title: Martyrdom of Polycarp
subtitle: eighty-six years his slave: Smyrna writes how its old overseer died
lead: The Martyrdom of Polycarp is a letter from the church at Smyrna, in the Roman province of Asia, to the church at Philomelium and 'to all the communities of the holy and catholic church in every place' (1:0). It tells how a persecution in Smyrna ended with the death of its aged overseer, Polycarp. It opens with the earlier martyrs, the brave Germanicus and Quintus, who gave himself up and then gave way (2-4). Then it follows Polycarp: his withdrawal to a farm and his vision of a burning pillow (5), his betrayal and arrest on a Friday (6-7), his refusal to say 'Lord Caesar' and sacrifice (8), his trial before the proconsul ('For eighty-six years I have been his slave', 9:3; 'I am a Christian', 10:1), the crowd's cry for fire (12), his prayer at the stake (14), the fire that would not burn him, the dagger and the dove (15-16), and the gathering of his bones and the plan to keep the yearly 'birthday of his martyrdom' (17-18). Closing notes give the date and the names of later copyists (19-22).

Lake calls it 'the earliest known history of a Christian martyrdom, the genuineness of which is unquestionable'; Bart Ehrman argues instead that it was written decades later by someone who claimed to have been there. It uses the Greek word for 'witness' throughout of one who dies for Christ, and it records the gathering of a martyr's bones and the plan to keep his day each year, which the Catholic Encyclopedia's article on relics calls 'the classical instance' of their veneration. No church counts it as Scripture. It is in no church's Bible.
facts: No church. It is not among the New Testament books listed by the Council of Trent, the Westminster Confession or the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, nor in Athanasius's Festal Letter 39; Article VI of the Church of England receives 'All the Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received', which do not include it. Eusebius quoted most of it as history (Church History 4.15).

The church of Smyrna. The writer named in 20:1 is Marcion in Lake's text (Marcus or Marcianus in other witnesses), and the scribe was Evarestus (20:2). Notes at the end name later copyists: Gaius, Socrates and Pionius (22:2-3).

Polycarp died on a Saturday, 23 February, under the proconsul Statius Quadratus (21:1): in 155 (Waddington), or 22 February 156 (Turner, Schwartz), or 166-167 (Eusebius's Chronicle, 'now ... almost universally abandoned'), as Lake's introduction reports. Lake calls the letter 'contemporary'; Bart Ehrman argues it was written decades later.
Smyrna (modern Izmir, Turkey), its stadium and the farms outside the city; written to Philomelium, a church that had asked for the story (20:1).
A letter that tells a martyr's arrest, trial and death, to be remembered and imitated. Lake: 'the earliest known history of a Christian martyrdom'.

Greek. Five Greek manuscripts in Lake (m, the Moscow codex of the 1200s, 'which has often the better text', against b p s v), Eusebius's quotation of most of it (Church History 4.15), a Latin version, and Syriac and Coptic extracts from Eusebius 'which have obviously no independent value' (Lake).

22 chapters: a greeting (1:0) and 53 sections. The Plain English Translation follows Lake's text throughout, with variant entries for the readings in his footnotes and the Moscow manuscript's other ending (22:2).
authorship: It speaks as 'we', the church of Smyrna (1:1), and its writers claim to have seen the end: 'we saw a wonder, we to whom it was given to see' (15:1). The summary was made 'through our brother Marcion' and written by Evarestus (20:1-2).
An 'obviously genuine and contemporary account' (Lake's introduction).

Bart Ehrman argues that the account 'was written decades later, by someone who wanted his readers to think he was an eyewitness': animal hunts in a 'stadium', 'a summary mock trial that does not follow any known legal precedent', likenesses to the passion that are 'literary touches, not historical recollections', and a dating note (21:1) whose officials, he says citing T. D. Barnes, do not fit one year (his blog, 2023, from Forgery and Counterforgery, 2013). The Catholic Encyclopedia, which accepts the letter, allows that the dating note may have been 'tampered with by a later hand'. Lake treats what follows 20:2 as notes added later.

audience.to: The church at Philomelium, which had asked for a full account of what happened at Smyrna (20:1), and through it the churches 'farther away' to which Philomelium was to send it on (20:1; 1:0). The church of Smyrna itself, which planned to gather every year at Polycarp's grave to keep 'the birthday of his martyrdom' (18:3), is the other first audience, and the later notes speak to copyists and readers of the next centuries (20:2-22:3).
audience.why: To tell the story, and to teach from it: a martyr should not seek death (4:1) or deny Christ (8-11), but wait for God's will and die 'in line with the gospel' (1:1; 19:1). It was written to churches that might face the same choice. Knowing that it was meant to be read at the yearly feast and passed from church to church explains its shape: a narrative to be remembered, with the lessons drawn out (2:1; 4:1; 17:3; 19:1).
views: A letter of Smyrna's church soon after Polycarp's death, by eyewitnesses (Lake: 'contemporary').
An account written decades later by someone who claimed to be an eyewitness, shaped on the passion to teach a view of martyrdom (Bart Ehrman).

outline: Greeting; a martyrdom in line with the gospel
The courage of the earlier martyrs
The arrest and the two-hour prayer
The trial: 'Eighty-six years'; 'I am a Christian'
The herald and the crowd's cry
The fire that would not burn him
His body, his bones and the yearly feast
Praise of Polycarp; send the letter on

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Reads the letter as a source: its date (155, 156 or later) and whether it is an eyewitness account (Lake) or a later one (Ehrman), its writer and scribe, which parts are later notes, the witnesses (the Moscow manuscript, the others, Eusebius, the Latin), and how far the passion parallels and the miracles shaped the story.

lenses.name: New Testament
lenses.desc: Follows the account's use of the Gospels and letters: the martyrdom 'in line with the gospel' (betrayal, Herod, the donkey, 'Your will be done', the cup), Revelation's letter to Smyrna, and the meaning of martys, 'witness'.

lenses.name: Martyrs and the saints
lenses.desc: Reads it as a martyr's story: the imitation of Christ, the rule against giving oneself up, the bones 'more precious than gems', the yearly 'birthday', and 'we worship him ... we love the martyrs', with the churches' views on honoring the saints taken from the site's cards.

lenses.name: Roman law and the city
lenses.desc: Reads it beside the Roman world: the proconsul and the stadium, the oath by Caesar's fortune and 'Lord Caesar', 'Away with the atheists', the Asiarch and the games, the police captain, and the crowd of Gentiles and Jews.

sections.b: The Plain English Translation is made from Kirsopp Lake's Greek (Loeb, 1913). Lake's text follows the Moscow manuscript where it is better; the variant entries give the readings his footnotes report and, from Eusebius's Greek, the places where Eusebius's copy differs. Key words follow the rest of the site: martys and its family are 'martyr', 'be martyred' and 'martyrdom' where they mean dying for Christ (with a note at 1:1); episkopos is 'overseer' (16:2, with a note); katholikos is 'catholic', lowercase (1:0); pais of Jesus is 'servant', with a gloss giving 'child', Lake's rendering (14:1; 14:3; 20:2); anthypatos is 'proconsul' as in Acts; Kyrios Kaisar is 'Lord Caesar', the Greek having no verb (8:2). The deaths and the tortures are told as plainly as the Greek tells them, adding nothing.

sections.h: Polycarp's life, as the sources tell it
sections.b: Lake: Polycarp was 'the Bishop of Smyrna in the first half of the second century', a disciple of John (whether the son of Zebedee or John the Elder, 'opinions differ'), martyred 'in all probability' on 23 February 155 at eighty-six. Irenaeus, who heard him as a boy, says apostles appointed him and that he visited Rome under Anicetus (Against Heresies 3.3.4); Eusebius preserves Irenaeus's memory of him teaching (Church History 5.20.5-8). His letter to the Philippians, also on this site, shows the pastor; this letter shows the martyr.

The note in 21:1 gives the day in three calendars: the second of Xanthicus (the Macedonian month used at Smyrna), seven days before the Kalends of March (23 February), and a 'great Sabbath'. Lake's introduction: Eusebius's date of 166-167 has been 'almost universally abandoned'; Waddington's dating of the proconsul Statius Quadratus to 153-154, with 23 February a Saturday in 155, gives 155; C. H. Turner and E. Schwartz argued from the 'great Sabbath' for 22 February 156. The Catholic Encyclopedia gives Waddington's year as 154-55, beginning in May. Bart Ehrman, citing T. D. Barnes, holds that the note's high priest and proconsul did not hold office in the same year. See the chapter page for 21.

The letter says almost everything happened so that the Lord might show 'a martyrdom in line with the gospel' (1:1), and it points out the likenesses: Polycarp waited to be handed over (1:2), was betrayed by his household (6:2), hunted by a Herod (6:2), arrested as if he were a bandit (7:1), said 'May God's will be done' (7:1), rode into the city on a donkey (8:1), and spoke of 'the cup of your Christ' (14:2). Lake: 'The coincidences are remarkable, but none are in themselves at all improbable.' Bart Ehrman: 'These are literary touches, not historical recollections.'

Eusebius (about 325) quotes 'the greater part of the letter' (Lake). In his Church History 4.15 (Greek read in Lake's Loeb edition, 1926), he quotes the greeting and first sentence (1:0-1, 4.15.3), retells 2:1-7:3 in his own words (4.15.4-14), quotes 8:1 to the first sentence of 19:1 (4.15.15-45), and stops there, so he has nothing of 19:1b-22:3. He adds that the same document carried other martyrdoms of Smyrna, among them Metrodorus, 'who appears to have been a proselyte of the Marcionitic sect' (4.15.46, NPNF). He puts the martyrdom under Marcus Aurelius (4.14.10-4.15.1).

His Greek differs from the manuscripts in many small words and in some that matter, each entered as a variant: 'holy catholic' without 'and' (1:0), no 'lawless Gentiles' (9:2), 'before his gray hair' for 'before his martyrdom' (13:2), a shorter opening to the prayer (14:1), no 'heavenly' and 'with him, in the Holy Spirit' (14:3), no loaf (15:2), a sword for the dagger and no dove (16:1), 'certain people' for the evil one as Nicetes' prompter and no 'blameless one for sinners' (17:2), and the Greek word for the Latin 'centurion' (18:1). He reads 'catholic' at 16:2.

Lake's five Greek manuscripts are m (Moscow 159, 1200s), b (Baroccianus 238, 1000s), p (Parisinus gr. 1452, 900s), s (Hierosolymitanus, 900s) and v (Vindobonensis, 1000s, ending with chapter 19); 'b p s v form a group as opposed to m, which has often the better text'.

sections.h: The copyists and the Moscow ending
sections.b: The notes at the end (22:2-3) say that Gaius copied the text from Irenaeus's (the Greek says 'from those of Irenaeus'), Socrates copied Gaius's copy in Corinth, and Pionius, after a vision of Polycarp, found it 'nearly worn out with age' and copied it again. Lake: 'Pionius, who is supposed to have lived in the 4th century'. The Moscow manuscript has a longer ending of its own (variant at 22:2): Irenaeus was in Rome when Polycarp died, taught many there, and heard 'a voice like a trumpet' saying 'Polycarp has been martyred'; it repeats Irenaeus's story of Marcion, and calls the Corinthian copyist Isocrates. The Catholic Encyclopedia judges that the postscript 'probably came from the pseudo-Pionius', the author of a later Life of Polycarp.

The letter's last chapters tell how Smyrna honored its martyr. The Christians want Polycarp's body 'to have a share in his holy flesh' (17:1); the officials fear they will 'start to worship this man'; the letter answers: 'For Christ we worship, because he is the Son of God. The martyrs we love as disciples and imitators of the Lord' (17:3). They gather his bones, 'worth more than costly gems' (18:2), and plan to keep 'the birthday of his martyrdom' each year (18:3). The Catholic Encyclopedia's article 'Relics' calls this 'the classical instance' of the veneration of relics and the 'keynote' of later writers in East and West; it quotes Harnack, from the other side, that 'Most offensive ... was the worship of relics'. How far the honor of saints may go is where the churches differ; the site's cards at 2 Kings 13 (relics), Acts 10 and Revelation 5 (honor and prayers of the saints) give each view.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the Asiarch's closed games and the haste of 13:1
spec.body: This is Claude's own reading of the text, not a published one as far as the sources opened here show. The crowd asked for a lion, but the Asiarch said he could not, 'since he had brought the animal hunts to a close' (12:2). The games were over, and the official in charge would not reopen them. So the crowd improvised a fire, gathering wood 'from the workshops and the baths' (13:1), the places nearest at hand that had fuel. That would explain the letter's stress on speed, 'faster than it could be told' (13:1), and why the execution looks so unlike a planned Roman sentence. The irregularities that Bart Ehrman takes as signs of a later writer (no formal trial, beasts in a 'stadium') would then be the marks of a mob's day.

prompts: 'Eighty-six years I have been his slave' (9:3)

In a crowded Roman stadium in Smyrna, under a hard afternoon sun, an old white-bearded man in a plain tunic stands calm before a seated Roman proconsul in a toga on a raised platform; the proconsul leans forward, one hand out, pleading; around them, rows of shouting spectators with raised fists; soldiers with spears; the old man's face turned slightly upward, peaceful.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, Egyptian hieroglyphic register lines and small glyph borders, plus a few bold flat shapes of lapis blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.

At the center of an arena, a great flame rises and bends into an arch, like a ship's sail swelling with wind, forming a glowing room of fire around an old man bound with his hands behind him at a wooden stake; he is untouched, shining like gold in a furnace; a few believers at the edge of the crowd kneel and stare; faint curling lines of incense-like smoke drift upward.

canon.summary: The Martyrdom of Polycarp is a letter of the church of Smyrna telling how its overseer Polycarp died, about 155-156 by the dates Lake reports. It is in no church's Bible. The Orthodox Church in America calls it 'one of the most ancient memorials of Christian literature' and keeps Polycarp's day on 23 February.
accepted_by: Not Scripture: the Council of Trent's list of New Testament books does not include it. The Catholic Encyclopedia retells Polycarp's death from the letter (Bacchus, 'St. Polycarp') and calls it 'the classical instance' of the early veneration of relics (Thurston, 'Relics').

Not part of the Bible. The Orthodox Church in America commemorates 'Hieromartyr Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna' on 23 February and, in its life of him, retells the account of the letter, which it calls 'one of the most ancient memorials of Christian literature', down to the vault of fire and the yearly feast. Its life puts the persecution under 'the emperor Marcus Aurelius (161-180)', with Eusebius, not in the 155-156 that Lake reports.
Not Scripture: the church's list of 35 New Testament books does not name it.
Not Scripture: Article VI receives 'All the Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received', which do not include it.
Not Scripture: the Westminster Confession lists the 27 books of the New Testament as Holy Scripture.

provenance.b: A letter of the church at Smyrna to Philomelium, written after Polycarp's death on a Saturday, 23 February, under the proconsul Statius Quadratus (21:1): 155 or 156 by the arguments Lake reports, who calls it 'contemporary'; Bart Ehrman argues for a writer decades later. It names its writer (Marcion, Marcus or Marcianus) and scribe (Evarestus) (20:1-2). What follows 20:2 is notes added later (Lake).

Five Greek manuscripts of the 900s-1200s in Lake's edition, Eusebius's quotation of 1:0-1 and 8:1-19:1 with a summary of 2-7 (Church History 4.15), and a Latin version. The copyists' notes trace the text from Irenaeus's copy through Gaius, Socrates and Pionius (22:2-3).

rejected_why.h: A church's report, not an apostle's book
rejected_why.b: The New Testament canon gathered writings held to come from the apostles and their circle. The Martyrdom is a letter of a second-century church about events of its own day, written long after the apostles; it makes no claim to apostolic authority. Eusebius used it as history, not Scripture: in his survey of accepted, disputed and rejected books (Church History 3.25) it does not appear, and he introduces it in book 4, saying that Polycarp's death, 'a written account of which is still extant, should be recorded in this history' (4.15.1, NPNF).

Its own purpose was the yearly remembrance at Polycarp's grave (18:3) and the strengthening of others who might face death. It was read as an account of a saint, as later churches read the acts of the martyrs, and never as one of the books of the Bible.

cited_in.b: The risen Christ's letter to Smyrna warns of prison and 'ten days of suffering' and promises 'the crown of life' to those faithful to death; the Martyrdom speaks of Polycarp 'crowned with the crown of incorruption' (17:1). The New Testament says nothing of Polycarp; the link is the city and the church, not a citation.

John's 'that Sabbath was a great day' and the Martyrdom's 'great Sabbath' (8:1; 21:1) say a like thing in different Greek (John megalē hē hēmera ekeinou tou sabbatou, the Martyrdom sabbatou megalou). Lake explains the Martyrdom's phrase as Purim or 'the Sabbath in the Passover week'; nothing shows that it borrows John's words. The Gospel does not refer to the account.
Lake's margin: the gospel teaching behind 'we give no praise to people who turn themselves in' (4:1). The account cites the Gospel's teaching, not the other way round.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to how Christians of the second century faced persecution, honored their martyrs and spoke of Christ, the letter is of the first importance. As a text it is well kept but not uniform: Eusebius's long quotation of about 325 agrees with the manuscripts in substance, but lacks some words that matter (the loaf, the dove, 'heavenly', 'the blameless one for sinners') and reads 'before his gray hair' at 13:2 and 'in the Holy Spirit' at 14:3. As history its outline (the arrest, the trial before Statius Quadratus, the burning, the date) is accepted by Lake and the Catholic Encyclopedia, while Bart Ehrman judges the account a later legend; its passion parallels and miracles (the voice, the fire, the dove) are weighed differently by readers. Its teaching agrees with the New Testament on Christ and on honoring rulers, and it records an honor for a martyr's remains that the churches weigh differently against the Bible.

sections.h: 1. As a witness to Christian faith and practice
sections.b: Very high. It shows how a church saw martyrdom (by God's will, not sought, 2:1; 4:1), how it prayed (14:1-3, ending with glory to the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit; Eusebius's copy: 'in the Holy Spirit'), how it spoke of the church as 'catholic' (8:1), of its leader as 'overseer' (16:2), and how it began to honor a martyr's bones and keep his yearly day (18:2-3).

Good. Lake: the text 'is quite good'. Five Greek manuscripts (900s-1200s), Eusebius's quotation of 'the greater part of the letter' (Lake) in the early 300s, and a Latin version. The manuscripts differ mostly in small words; Eusebius's Greek, read in Lake's Loeb edition, differs from them in several places that change the sense. The variant entries give them (1:0, 2:2, 2:3, 7:1, 9:2, 13:2, 14:1-3, 15:2, 16:1-2, 17:2, 18:1, 19:2, 20:1-2, 22:1-3). The notes after 20:2 are later additions, and the Moscow manuscript has its own ending.

The account names officials, places and a date, and Lake judges it contemporary. Readers differ on three things. First, the likenesses to Jesus' passion: the writer says he shows them (1:1); Lake thinks none is improbable; Bart Ehrman takes them as 'literary touches'. Second, the setting and the date: Ehrman finds beasts in a 'stadium' and a 'summary mock trial' impossible as history and, citing T. D. Barnes, holds that the high priest and proconsul of 21:1 did not serve in one year; the Catholic Encyclopedia, which accepts the date, allows that the note may have been 'tampered with by a later hand'. Third, the wonders: the voice heard only by Christians (9:1), the vision fulfilled (5:2; 12:3), the fire that formed a vault and did not burn (15:2), and the dove (16:1), missing in Eusebius and doubted by Wordsworth. Christians who accept that God works miracles can read them as signs given to strengthen the church; others treat them as the writers' faith-filled way of seeing an extraordinary death.

Matches: worship of Christ alone as Son of God (17:2-3; John 20:28); honor to rulers 'appointed by God' (10:2; Romans 13:1); the fear of the eternal fire rather than the brief one (11:2; Matthew 10:28); not seeking martyrdom but fleeing when possible (4:1; 5:1; Matthew 10:23); resurrection of soul and body (14:2; John 5:29). Goes beyond: the martyrs as 'already angels' (2:3); the gathering of a martyr's bones as 'worth more than costly gems' and a yearly feast at his grave (18:2-3). The Bible tells of Joseph's bones carried out of Egypt (Genesis 50:25; Exodus 13:19) and of the dead man who touched Elisha's bones (2 Kings 13:21), but not of a church keeping a martyr's bones or his day; the churches read these passages differently (the site's cards at 2 Kings 13, Acts 10 and Revelation 5). Conflicts: none in its teaching about God and Christ. Its blame of 'the Jews' as a people, 'as is their habit' (13:1), is hard to reconcile with Paul's insistence that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1-2, 28-29), though harsh words about 'the Jews' already appear in 1 Thessalonians 2:14-16; see the topic on Christian anti-Judaism.

how_to_read.h: As a letter meant to be imitated
how_to_read.b: The writers say what they want the reader to learn: wait for God's will, do not give yourself up, do not deny Christ, and follow 'in his footsteps' (1:1-2; 4:1; 19:1; 22:1). Read the story with those lessons in view.

Notice each likeness to Jesus' passion that the writer points out (the notes mark them), and notice the differences: Polycarp is not crucified, he is not silent, and his death saves no one. The account means him as a follower, 'a disciple and imitator of the Lord' (17:3).

Polycarp to the Philippians, also on this site, shows the man in his own words: a pastor who urged a church to imitate Christ's endurance (Polycarp to the Philippians 8:2) and honored the martyrs who 'ran in faith and righteousness' (Polycarp to the Philippians 9:2). The Martyrdom shows him doing what he taught.
